question: What document allows an operator to carry out commercial air transport?

options.text: An airport operating licence issued by each destination

explanation: Commercial air transport may only be undertaken by an approved operator in accordance with an air operator certificate issued by the authority.

question: Which authority issues an operator's AOC?

options.text: The authority of the State where most of its passengers live
The authority of the State of Registry of its first aircraft
The authority of every State it flies to
The State of its principal place of business

explanation: The AOC is issued by the authority of the State in which the operator has its principal place of business.

question: May an applicant for an AOC already hold an AOC from another authority?

options.text: Only if both AOCs are for cargo operations

explanation: An applicant must not already hold an AOC issued by another authority unless specifically approved by the authorities concerned.

question: Where must the aeroplanes used under an AOC normally be registered?

options.text: In the State issuing the AOC
In any State the operator chooses
In the State where they are maintained

explanation: Aeroplanes must normally be registered in the State issuing the AOC; by mutual agreement of the authorities, aeroplanes registered in another State may be used.

question: What must an applicant's organisation and management structure match?

options.text: The number of routes planned in the first year
The size of the main operating base building
The scale and scope of the operation
The structure of the national airline

explanation: The applicant must satisfy the authority that its organisation and management structure are suitable and matched to the scale (size) and scope (types of operation) of the undertaking.

question: How must an AOC holder have its aeroplanes maintained?

options.text: By an approved organisation, to an approved programme
By any engineer with a licence
By the flight crew, if they hold an engineering licence

explanation: Aeroplanes must be airworthy and maintained to an approved maintenance programme by an approved maintenance organisation, either the operator itself (if approved) or a third party that is approved.

question: When may the authority vary, suspend or revoke an AOC?

options.text: Whenever the operator's ticket prices change
When it doubts the operation is safe

explanation: At the authority's discretion, an AOC may be varied, revoked or suspended if it ceases to be satisfied that the operator can continue to operate safely.

question: What do the authority's periodic audits of an operator include?

options.text: Only the flight crew's licences and medical certificates

explanation: The authority's periodic audits include inspection of the operator's own internal audit system and of its financial records.

question: Where must any limitations imposed by the authority on an operator be stated?

options.text: Only in the operator's quality manual
Only in a letter kept at the main base

explanation: Any limitations or restrictions imposed by the authority must be stated on the certificate, and the operator must respect them.

question: Who is responsible to the authority for compliance with all the AOC requirements?
explanation: The accountable manager, nominated by the operator and acceptable to the authority, is responsible for ensuring all operations and maintenance can be financed and carried out to the required standard.

question: What is the accountable manager specifically responsible for?

options.text: Funding operations and maintenance to the standard
Flying the first flight of each new type
Approving every crew roster in person

explanation: The accountable manager ensures all operations and maintenance activities can be financed and carried out to the standard required by the authority.

question: Which of these is a nominated post holder required by the authority?
explanation: The required nominated post holders are for flight operations, the maintenance system, crew training and ground operations.

question: An operator has 21 or more full-time employees. How many people at least must fill the four nominated posts?
explanation: For operators with 21 or more full-time employees, a minimum of two persons must fill the four positions. One person may hold more than one post if acceptable to the authority.

question: In a small operator (fewer than 20 full-time staff), who may hold one or more of the nominated posts?

options.text: No one; the posts must be left vacant
Any pilot with more than 1000 hours

explanation: For operators with fewer than 20 full-time employees, the accountable manager may fill one or more of the posts if the authority accepts it.

subtopic: Main base, aeroplanes and other conditions
question: What does the authority require at the operator's main operating base?

options.text: A maintenance hangar for every aircraft
An office of the authority on the premises
A runway of at least 3000 m

explanation: The authority requires full operational support facilities at the main operating base, appropriate to the area and type of operation.

subtopic: Main base, aeroplanes and other conditions
question: What certificate of airworthiness must aeroplanes used under an AOC have?
explanation: The aeroplanes must have a standard certificate of airworthiness issued in accordance with the international airworthiness standard.

subtopic: Main base, aeroplanes and other conditions
question: What may the authority require if it is not satisfied that the requirements for an AOC are met?

options.text: A change of the company name
Ground school for all the operator's managers

explanation: If not satisfied, the authority may require demonstration flights flown as if they were full commercial air transport flights.

subtopic: Main base, aeroplanes and other conditions
question: After applying for an AOC, what must the operator do if any required information changes?

options.text: Nothing; the application is fixed once submitted
Start a new application from scratch
Wait until the next annual audit to mention it

explanation: Once the application has been submitted, the operator must notify the authority of any changes to the required information or procedures.

question: Which of these does an AOC specify?

options.text: The fares charged on each route
The names of the operator's pilots
The routes and timetable for the season

explanation: The AOC specifies the operator's name and location, dates of issue and validity, types of operation, aircraft types and registrations, authorised areas of operation, special limitations, and special approvals.

question: Which of these is a special authorisation that may be shown on an AOC?
explanation: Special authorisations include CAT II/III (with minima), operations in high-level oceanic specification airspace, ETOPS, RNAV, RVSM, carriage of dangerous goods and authority to give cabin crew initial safety training.

question: Which special approval on an AOC includes the approved minima?
explanation: The CAT II/III authorisation on the AOC includes the approved minima.

question: What is an adequate aerodrome?

options.text: One judged satisfactory, with services available
An aerodrome with a precision approach and a fire service open 24 hours
Any aerodrome listed in the State's AIP
Any aerodrome with a paved runway

explanation: An adequate aerodrome is one the operator considers satisfactory, considering performance requirements and runway characteristics, that at the expected time of use is available and has ATS, lighting, communications, weather reporting, navaids and emergency services.

question: What extra does an adequate ETOPS en route alternate need beyond being an adequate aerodrome?

options.text: Customs and immigration available at all hours
A runway of at least 3000 m

explanation: An adequate ETOPS en route alternate is an adequate aerodrome that, at the expected time of use, also has an ATS facility and at least one instrument approach procedure.

question: What is ETOPS?

options.text: Flight over the polar regions only
Twins flying beyond a threshold from an adequate aerodrome
Any long-range operation by a four-engine aeroplane
An approved procedure for engine-out take-offs from short runways

explanation: ETOPS operations are those with approved two-engine aeroplanes operating beyond the threshold distance from an adequate aerodrome.

question: What is a 3% ERA?

options.text: An alternate that may be used only 3% of the time
An en route alternate selected to reduce contingency fuel to 3%
An aerodrome whose runway slope is 3%
An aerodrome within 3% of the route length from the destination

explanation: A 3% ERA is an en route alternate aerodrome selected so that contingency fuel can be reduced to 3% of trip fuel.

question: For a turbine aeroplane, when may a destination be treated as an isolated aerodrome?

options.text: When it is more than 500 NM from any other aerodrome
When it has only one runway
When the fuel to the alternate exceeds 45 minutes of holding
When alternate plus final reserve fuel exceeds 2 hours

explanation: For turbine aeroplanes, a destination may be treated as isolated if the fuel required to go to the nearest adequate destination alternate is more than two hours at normal cruise consumption above the destination, including final reserve fuel.

question: For a piston aeroplane, what fuel figure makes a destination an isolated aerodrome?

options.text: 45 minutes plus 15% of the cruise time, or 2 hours, whichever of the two is greater
2 hours at holding speed, including reserve
45 min + 15% of cruise time, or 2 h if less

explanation: For reciprocating-engine aeroplanes, the figure is fuel for 45 minutes plus 15% of the flight time planned at cruising level, or two hours, whichever is less.

question: How far from the threshold must an "equivalent position" for an approach be?
explanation: An equivalent position is a fix established by DME, NDB, VOR, SRE, PAR or another suitable fix between three and five miles from the threshold.

question: Which of these is defined as a critical phase of flight?

options.text: The take-off run and flight path
Taxiing to the stand after landing

explanation: Critical phases of flight are the take-off run, the take-off flight path, the final approach, the landing including the landing roll, and any other phases at the commander's discretion.

question: What is contingency fuel for?

options.text: Flying from the destination to the alternate

explanation: Contingency fuel compensates for unforeseen factors affecting consumption to the destination, such as deviations from expected consumption, forecast weather, planned routing or levels.

question: What are "separate runways"?

options.text: Runways where one blocked does not stop the other
Parallel runways at least 1000 m apart
The two ends of the same runway, used in opposite directions

explanation: Separate runways are separate landing surfaces at the same aerodrome which may overlay or cross, but if one is blocked the planned operations on the other can continue. Each must have its own approach based on a separate navigation aid.

question: What must each of two "separate runways" have?

options.text: A length of at least 2000 m and its own taxiway
Its own approach on its own navaid

explanation: Each runway must have a separate approach procedure based on a separate navigation aid.

question: Who selects the approved one-engine-inoperative cruise speed for ETOPS?
explanation: The approved one-engine-inoperative cruise speed is selected by the operator, within the aeroplane's certified limits, and approved by the authority.

question: What is an ETOPS area?

options.text: The airspace within 60 minutes of the departure aerodrome
Airspace above FL290 over the oceans
Any area where only twins may fly
Airspace beyond the set one-engine-out time from an alternate

explanation: An ETOPS area contains airspace in which an approved aeroplane is more than the specified flying time, in still air at the approved one-engine-inoperative cruise speed, from an adequate ETOPS en route alternate.

question: Until when do ETOPS planning minima apply?

options.text: Until the aircraft reaches cruising level

explanation: ETOPS planning minima apply until dispatch, which is when the aircraft first moves under its own power for the purpose of taking off.

question: How many parts does the operations manual have?

options.text: Four: A, B, C and D
Five, the last part being for cabin crew

explanation: The operations manual has four parts: A (general), B (aeroplane operating matters), C (route and aerodrome information) and D (training).

question: Which part of the operations manual contains flight time limitations and the quality system?

options.text: Part C, route and aerodrome information
Part A, general and basic information

explanation: Part A covers administration, organisation, operational control, the quality system, crew composition, qualifications, health precautions, flight time limitations, operating procedures, dangerous goods, security, occurrence reporting, rules of the air and leasing.

question: Which part of the operations manual contains the MEL and the aeroplane's performance information?

options.text: Part A, general and basic information
Part C, route and aerodrome information

explanation: Part B contains limitations, normal, abnormal and emergency procedures, performance, flight planning, mass and balance, loading, CDL, MEL, emergency equipment, evacuation procedures and systems.

question: Where would aerodrome operating minima be found in the operations manual?
explanation: Part C contains route and aerodrome instructions and information, including aerodrome operating minima.

question: What does Part D of the operations manual contain?
explanation: Part D covers training methods and requirements so that all personnel are competent.

question: Who must approve the operations manual?
explanation: The operator must ensure the operations manual is approved by the authority, contains all the instructions personnel need, and does not contravene the AOC or regulations.

question: In which language must the operations manual normally be prepared?

options.text: The language of the State of Design
The native language of most of the operator's pilots

explanation: The operations manual must be in English unless otherwise approved by the authority or prescribed by national law. It may be translated in full or part.

question: Which parts of the operations manual must each crew member be given a personal copy of, or relevant sections from?
explanation: Crew members must be supplied with a personal copy of, or sections from, Parts A and B.

question: When must the authority receive a proposed amendment to the operations manual?

options.text: In advance of the effective date
Within 30 days after it takes effect
Only if the amendment concerns dangerous goods

explanation: The authority must be supplied with any proposed amendment in advance of its effective date; if approval is required, it must be obtained before the amendment takes effect.

question: When may an urgent operations manual amendment be published immediately?

options.text: For safety, with the authority's permission
Never; all amendments wait for approval
Whenever the amendment is shorter than one page
Whenever the chief pilot signs it

explanation: If an amendment must be immediate in the interest of safety, it may be published immediately provided the authority grants permission.

question: Which design principles must the operations manual follow?

options.text: Alphabetical order of all subjects in a single volume

explanation: The contents must be presented in a form that can be used without difficulty and the design must observe human factors principles.

question: What must the operator ensure about all personnel involved in ground and flight operations?

options.text: They have worked for the operator for at least a year
They are trained and competent in their duties
They have passed the same medical examination as pilots

explanation: All such personnel must be properly instructed, have demonstrated their abilities in their duties, and be aware of their responsibilities and how they fit the whole operation.

question: Must the pre-flight inspection be carried out by the approved maintenance organisation?

options.text: Only on the first flight of the day

explanation: Aeroplanes are maintained and released to service by an approved organisation, but the pre-flight inspection need not necessarily be done by it; flight crew commonly carry it out.
